title: Two streams of water
told: as the old texts tell it

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? on your birthday, do you like a big celebration, or a quiet one?
options: then you’ll love this festival. listen.
this one has quiet mornings too. listen.
fair. this birthday is about more than a birthday.

steps.line: Long ago, a queen named Maya was traveling to her parents’ home when she stopped to rest in a garden called Lumbini.
There, standing beneath a flowering sal tree, holding one of its branches, she gave birth to a son.
The old texts say the newborn stood, took seven steps, and spoke: this is my last birth.
steps.label: as the old texts tell it

steps.q: Two streams of water fall from the sky to bathe the newborn. What are they like, the old texts say?
steps.why: One cool and one warm, for the baby and his mother. That’s the moment people re-enact today.

steps.line: Then two streams of water fell from the sky, one cool and one warm, to bathe him.
steps.label: as the old texts tell it

steps.line: Today, in many East Asian temples, people pour water over a small statue of the baby Buddha, one hand pointing up.
steps.label: today

steps.line: And in Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar, the full moon of Vesak marks three things at once: his birth, his awakening and his death.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Why would one festival hold his birth, his awakening and his death together?
o: Tradition puts all three on the same full moon
Nobody knew his birthday, so they merged them
A king joined the three feasts into one
steps.why: Theravada tradition holds that he was born, woke up and died on the full moon of the month Vesakha, in different years. One night, three anniversaries.

steps.q: A man once asked the Buddha: are you a god? A spirit? A human? What did he answer?
o: A god born as a man
None of those. Remember me as awake.
steps.why: In the Dona Sutta he says no to each, and asks to be remembered as buddha, awake. It’s a title, not a name.

steps.q: In Japan, on his birthday each April, what do people pour over the little statue?
o: Water drawn from the temple well
steps.why: Amacha, a sweet hydrangea tea, at Hana Matsuri, the flower festival. It recalls the sweet rain that, in East Asian tellings, nine dragons poured at his birth.

say: vesak is a spring full moon. in many theravada countries it marks his birth, awakening and death together. in japan the birthday has its own flower festival in april, and much of east asia remembers the other two on other days.
different calendars, the same life. and the one everyone is celebrating, by his own account, wasn’t a god. he was a person who woke up.

steps.q: The newborn said, “This is my last birth.” Why does that line matter so much to Buddhists?
o: He would wake up and never be reborn again
He knew he would die young
He would be the last buddha ever
steps.why: Buddhists hope to end the cycle of rebirth, and “last birth” means this is the life he wakes up for good. Tradition says another buddha, Metteyya, is still to come.

today.say: on vesak, many buddhists light lanterns and do good deeds in the buddha’s honor. today, if you like, light a lamp or a candle and remember him as he asked: a person who woke up. then do one kind thing in his honor.
options: then a little of vesak is in your home.
that’s how many buddhists keep vesak. lovely.

tomorrow.title: One lamp lights another
tomorrow.line: a king asks a monk what carries on after we die. the monk answers with a lamp.
